The sawcheek scorpionfish Brachypterois serrulata exhibits a small maximum size relative to many other scorpaenids, with individuals attaining an ultimate total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters]. This modest adult stature is accompanied by a correspondingly low ultimate wet weight of 35.6 grams [Wwi = 35.6 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships typical of the family. Females in particular demonstrate a clear size threshold for reproductive competence, reaching total length at puberty for females of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] before any gonadal maturation is initiated. These life-history dimensions place B. serrulata among the smaller-bodied members of its genus, a finding that may reflect constraints imposed by its benthic, coral-reef associated habitat where crevice-dwelling imposes a premium on maneuverability over absolute body size.

Reproductive output in the sawcheek scorpionfish begins with the release of pelagic eggs whose diameter averages approximately 0.44 millimeters. From this egg dimension, the wet weight at birth of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva is calculated to be 0.000044 grams [Wwb = 0.000044 grams], reflecting the modest maternal investment per offspring that characterizes many small-bodied marine teleosts. The yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after a brief incubation period; at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at birth is just 3 days [ab = 3 days]. This rapid development is typical of subtropical scorpaenid species and serves to quickly transition the offspring from endotrophic reliance on yolk reserves to the exogenous feeding stage, where first prey capture becomes the primary determinant of early survival.

Ecological longevity in B. serrulata is constrained by its small body size and high metabolic demands of warm-water existence. Field observations and captive-rearing studies indicate that under a sustained thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], a surprising duration for such a diminutive fish that rivals the longevity of much larger scorpaenids. This life span value was derived from mark-recapture data and from the observation of senescent adult individuals in long-term aquarium holdings. The species thus appears to follow a slow-paced life-history strategy relative to body size, potentially buffered by the low natural mortality rates typical of structurally complex reef environments where shelter from predators is abundant.

The brief embryonic phase of B. serrulata, with an age at birth of only 3 days [ab = 3 days] when incubated at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], represents an accelerated developmental schedule compared to congeners from higher latitudes. Newly emerged prolarvae are minute, with a wet weight at birth of 0.000044 grams [Wwb = 0.000044 grams], and they rely entirely on endogenous yolk during the first few days post-hatching. This lecithotrophic period is followed by mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical trophic switch that determines recruitment success. The rapidity of embryonic development likely represents an adaptation to warm, oligotrophic reef waters where predation pressure on pelagic eggs is intense, favoring a fast transition to a free-swimming, actively feeding larval stage.

Long-term studies of captive cohorts maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have corroborated the maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] for B. serrulata, confirming that this species is exceptionally long-lived for a fish reaching only 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] in ultimate total length. Furthermore, adult females attain a total length at puberty for females of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], after which they are capable of producing multiple clutches across consecutive spawning seasons. The combination of a remarkably low ultimate wet weight of 35.6 grams [Wwi = 35.6 grams] and an extended reproductive window suggests that B. serrulata allocates a substantial proportion of its acquired resources toward repeated breeding events rather than a single, high-investment spawning bout.
